concepts.title: Variables
concepts.text:
A **variable** is a named box that stores a value in memory. You create it by assigning a value; later you can read or change it.
- Python is dynamically typed: the type comes from the value (`x = 5`).
- Java and C++ are statically typed: you declare the type (`int x = 5;`).
- JavaScript uses `let` (changeable), `const` (cannot be reassigned) and the old `var`.

code.python:
name = "Asha"      # str
age = 21           # int
age = age + 1      # reassign
print(name, age)   # Asha 22

concepts.title: Data types
concepts.text:
A **data type** says what kind of value a variable holds and which operations are allowed.
- **Python:** `int`, `float`, `complex`, `bool`, `str`, `list`, `tuple`, `dict`, `set`, `NoneType`. Check with `type(x)`.
- **JavaScript:** primitives `number`, `bigint`, `string`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `symbol` + `object` (arrays and functions are objects). Check with `typeof x`.
- **Java:** 8 primitives `byte short int long float double char boolean` + reference types such as `String`, arrays and classes.
- **C++:** `int`, `long long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `bool`, plus `string`, arrays, `vector`, structs and classes.
- **SQL:** `INT`, `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `VARCHAR(n)`, `CHAR(n)`, `DATE`, `BOOLEAN`, `TEXT`…

code.python:
print(type(10), type(3.5), type("hi"), type(True), type(None))
# <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'str'> <class 'bool'> <class 'NoneType'>
code.javascript:
console.log(typeof 10, typeof "hi", typeof true, typeof undefined, typeof null);
// number string boolean undefined object
code.java: int a = 10; double b = 3.5; char c = 'A'; boolean d = true; String s = "hi";
code.cpp:
int a = 10; double b = 3.5; char c = 'A'; bool d = true; string s = "hi";
cout << sizeof(int) << endl; // usually 4 (bytes)

concepts.title: Operators
concepts.text:
**Operators** combine values.
- Arithmetic: `+ - * /`, remainder `%`, Python also has floor division `//` and power `**`.
- Comparison: `== != < > <= >=` (JavaScript prefers strict `===` / `!==`).
- Logical: Python `and or not`; JS/Java/C++ `&& || !`.
- Assignment: `= += -= *= /=`; JS/Java/C++ have `++` and `--`.
- **Precedence** (high → low): `**` → unary minus → `* / // %` → `+ -` → comparisons → `not` → `and` → `or`.
- Integer division differs: Python `7 // 2 = 3` and `7 / 2 = 3.5`; Java/C++ `7 / 2 = 3` for ints; JavaScript `7 / 2 = 3.5`.

code.python:
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 3)   # 3.5 3 1 8
print(5 > 3 and 2 > 4)               # False
print(-7 // 2)                        # -4 (floors toward -infinity)
code.javascript:
console.log(7 / 2, Math.floor(7 / 2), 7 % 2, 2 ** 3); // 3.5 3 1 8
console.log(5 == "5", 5 === "5");                      // true false
code.java:
System.out.println(7 / 2);   // 3  (int division)
System.out.println(7 / 2.0); // 3.5
System.out.println(7 % 2);   // 1
int i = 5; System.out.println(i++ + " " + ++i); // 5 7

concepts.title: Input and output
concepts.text:
How each language prints and reads values:
- **Python:** `print()` to show, `input()` to read (always returns a `str` — convert with `int()` / `float()`).
- **JavaScript:** `console.log()`; in a browser `prompt()`, in Node use `readline`.
- **Java:** `System.out.println()`; read with `Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)`.
- **C++:** `cout << x;` and `cin >> x;` from `<iostream>`.

code.python:
name = input("Your name: ")
age = int(input("Age: "))
print("Hi", name, "next year you will be", age + 1)
print("a", "b", sep="-", end="!\n")   # a-b!
code.javascript:
console.log("Hi", 42);
console.log(`Template: ${2 + 3}`);   // Template: 5

concepts.title: Type conversion (casting)
concepts.text:
**Type conversion** changes a value from one type to another.
- Implicit: the language converts automatically (e.g. `int + float → float`).
- Explicit (casting): you ask for it.

code.python:
print(int("42") + 1)     # 43
print(str(10) + "5")     # 105
print(float("3.5"), int(3.99))  # 3.5 3 (truncates)
print(list("abc"))       # ['a', 'b', 'c']
code.javascript:
console.log(Number("42") + 1, parseInt("12px"), String(10) + 5); // 43 12 "105"
console.log("5" * 2, "5" + 2);  // 10 "52"

concepts.title: Comments
concepts.text:
Comments are notes for humans; the computer ignores them.
- Python: `# single line`, and `"""docstrings"""` for documenting functions.
- JavaScript / Java / C++: `// single line` and `/* multi-line */`. Java also has `/** Javadoc */`.
- SQL: `-- single line` and `/* multi-line */`.

concepts.title: Scope (local vs global)
concepts.text:
**Scope** is where a variable can be seen.
- A variable created inside a function is **local** — it disappears when the function ends.
- A variable created outside all functions is **global**.
- Python needs `global x` to reassign a global inside a function (and `nonlocal` for an enclosing function's variable).
- JS `let`/`const` and Java/C++ variables are **block-scoped** (visible only inside the `{ }` where they were declared).

code.python:
count = 0
def bump():
    global count
    count += 1
bump(); bump()
print(count)   # 2

concepts.title: Strings
concepts.text:
A **string** is a sequence of characters.
- Index from 0 (`s[0]`); Python also allows negative indexes (`s[-1]` = last char).
- Strings are **immutable** in Python, Java and JavaScript — methods return a *new* string.
- Common methods: upper/lower case, trim/strip spaces, replace, split into a list, join, find/indexOf, startswith/endsWith, slicing/substring, length.
- Ask me about any single method, e.g. *"what does split do in Python"*.

code.python:
s = "  Hello World  "
print(s.strip().upper())      # HELLO WORLD
print(s.split())              # ['Hello', 'World']
print("-".join(["a", "b"]))   # a-b
print("python"[::-1])         # nohtyp
print(len("code"), "code".find("d"))  # 4 2
code.javascript:
const s = "  Hello World  ";
console.log(s.trim().toUpperCase());  // HELLO WORLD
console.log("a,b,c".split(","));      // ["a","b","c"]
console.log("code".slice(1, 3), "code".length); // od 4
console.log([..."abc"].reverse().join(""));   // cba
code.java:
String s = "  Hello World  ";
System.out.println(s.trim().toUpperCase());   // HELLO WORLD
System.out.println("code".substring(1, 3));   // od
System.out.println("code".charAt(0) + " " + "code".length()); // c 4
System.out.println(new StringBuilder("abc").reverse()); // cba
code.cpp:
string s = "Hello World";
cout << s.size() << " " << s.substr(0, 5) << endl; // 11 Hello
cout << s.find("World") << endl;                   // 6
reverse(s.begin(), s.end()); cout << s << endl;    // dlroW olleH
code.sql: SELECT UPPER(name), LENGTH(name), SUBSTR(name, 1, 3), name || '!' FROM users;

concepts.title: Slicing / substrings
concepts.text:
**Slicing** takes a part of a sequence: `s[start:stop:step]` in Python — `stop` is **excluded**.
- `s[:3]` first 3, `s[-3:]` last 3, `s[::2]` every 2nd, `s[::-1]` reversed.
- JavaScript: `s.slice(start, end)`; Java: `s.substring(start, end)`; C++: `s.substr(start, length)` (note: length, not end!).

code.python:
t = "programming"
print(t[0:3], t[-4:], t[::3], t[::-1])
# pro ming pgmn gnimmargorp
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:4])   # [20, 30, 40]
code.java:
String t = "programming";
System.out.println(t.substring(0, 3) + " " + t.substring(t.length() - 4)); // pro ming
code.cpp:
string t = "programming";
cout << t.substr(0, 3) << " " << t.substr(t.size() - 4) << endl; // pro ming

concepts.title: Python lists
concepts.text:
A **list** is an ordered, **mutable** collection that can hold mixed types: `[1, "a", True]`.
- Add: `append(x)` (one item), `extend(iterable)` (many), `insert(i, x)`.
- Remove: `remove(x)` (first match by value), `pop(i)` (by index, returns it), `del lst[i]`, `clear()`.
- Other: `sort()`, `reverse()`, `index(x)`, `count(x)`, `copy()`; built-ins `len`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted`.
- `sort()` changes the list and returns `None`; `sorted(lst)` returns a new list.

code.python:
nums = [4, 1, 3]
nums.append(10)       # [4, 1, 3, 10]
nums.extend([7, 8])   # [4, 1, 3, 10, 7, 8]
nums.insert(0, 99)    # [99, 4, 1, 3, 10, 7, 8]
nums.remove(3)        # removes value 3
last = nums.pop()     # 8
nums.sort()
print(nums, last)     # [1, 4, 7, 10, 99] 8
print(sum(nums), max(nums), len(nums))  # 121 99 5

concepts.title: Arrays
concepts.text:
An **array** stores many values of the same kind under one name, accessed by index (starting at 0).
- **JavaScript arrays** are dynamic: `push/pop` (end), `unshift/shift` (start), `splice`, `slice`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `includes`, `indexOf`, `sort`, `join`.
- **Java arrays** have a fixed size (`int[] a = new int[5]`); use `Arrays.sort`, `Arrays.toString`; for a growable list use `ArrayList`.
- **C++** raw arrays are fixed (`int a[5]`); prefer `vector<int>` which grows with `push_back`.
- In **Python** the list plays the role of an array.

code.javascript:
const a = [5, 2, 9];
a.push(4);                        // [5, 2, 9, 4]
const doubled = a.map((x) => x * 2); // [10, 4, 18, 8]
const big = a.filter((x) => x > 4);  // [5, 9]
const total = a.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0); // 20
a.sort((x, y) => x - y);          // numeric sort! [2, 4, 5, 9]
code.python:
arr = [5, 2, 9]
arr.append(4)
print(sorted(arr))            # [2, 4, 5, 9]
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(matrix[1][0])           # 3

concepts.title: Tuples
concepts.text:
A **tuple** is an ordered, **immutable** collection: `(1, 2, 3)`.
- Faster and safer than a list when data must not change (e.g. coordinates, RGB colours, dictionary keys).
- Only two methods: `count(x)` and `index(x)`.
- A one-item tuple needs a comma: `(5,)` — `(5)` is just the number 5.
- **Packing/unpacking:** `a, b = b, a` swaps two variables.
- C++ has `pair` and `tuple`; Java has no built-in tuple (use a record/class).

code.python:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point               # unpacking
print(x + y)               # 7
t = (1, 2, 2, 3)
print(t.count(2), t.index(3))  # 2 3
single = (5,)
print(type(single))        # <class 'tuple'>
# point[0] = 9  -> TypeError: tuple does not support item assignment

concepts.title: Dictionaries / maps
concepts.text:
A **dictionary (map)** stores **key → value** pairs; keys are unique.
- **Python dict:** `d[key]`, `d.get(key, default)`, `keys()`, `values()`, `items()`, `update()`, `pop(key)`, `setdefault()`. Keys must be immutable (str, int, tuple).
- **JavaScript:** plain objects `{ name: "Asha" }` or `Map` (`set/get/has/delete/size`).
- **Java:** `HashMap<K,V>` with `put/get/getOrDefault/containsKey/remove`; `TreeMap` keeps keys sorted.
- **C++:** `map` (sorted) and `unordered_map` (hash, faster average).

concepts.title: Sets
concepts.text:
A **set** is an **unordered** collection of **unique** items — perfect for removing duplicates and fast membership tests.
- Python: `add`, `update`, `remove` (error if missing), `discard` (no error), `pop`, and maths: `|` union, `&` intersection, `-` difference, `^` symmetric difference. Empty set is `set()` — `{}` is an empty *dict*!
- JavaScript: `new Set()` with `add/has/delete/size`.
- Java: `HashSet`, sorted `TreeSet`. C++: `set` (sorted), `unordered_set`, `multiset` (allows duplicates).

concepts.title: ArrayList & the Collections framework (Java)
concepts.text:
`ArrayList<T>` is a resizable array. Main methods: `add(x)`, `add(i, x)`, `get(i)`, `set(i, x)`, `remove(i)` / `remove(Object)`, `size()`, `contains(x)`, `indexOf(x)`, `isEmpty()`, `clear()`, `sort(null)`.
- `Collections` utility methods: `Collections.sort(list)`, `reverse`, `max`, `min`, `frequency`, `shuffle`.
- Other collections: `LinkedList` (fast insert/remove at ends), `HashSet` (unique), `HashMap` (key → value), `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` (sorted), `ArrayDeque` (stack/queue).
- Collections hold objects, so use wrapper types: `ArrayList<Integer>`, not `ArrayList<int>`.

concepts.title: Comprehensions
concepts.text: A **comprehension** builds a list/dict/set in one readable line: `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`.

concepts.title: Stack and queue
concepts.text:
- **Stack** = LIFO (last in, first out) — like a pile of plates. Operations: push, pop, peek/top.
- **Queue** = FIFO (first in, first out) — like a ticket line. Operations: enqueue, dequeue, front.
- Python: list as stack (`append`/`pop`), `collections.deque` as queue (`append`/`popleft`).
- Java: `ArrayDeque` (`push/pop` or `offer/poll`). C++: `stack<int>`, `queue<int>`, `priority_queue<int>`.

code.python:
from collections import deque
stack = [1, 2]; stack.append(3); print(stack.pop())   # 3
q = deque([1, 2]); q.append(3); print(q.popleft())    # 1
code.cpp:
stack<int> st; st.push(1); st.push(2); cout << st.top() << endl; // 2
queue<int> q; q.push(1); q.push(2); cout << q.front() << endl;   // 1
code.java:
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>(); st.push(1); st.push(2); System.out.println(st.pop()); // 2
Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>(); q.offer(1); q.offer(2); System.out.println(q.poll()); // 1
code.javascript:
const st = [1, 2]; st.push(3); console.log(st.pop());   // 3
const q = [1, 2]; q.push(3); console.log(q.shift());    // 1

concepts.title: Conditional statements
concepts.text:
**Conditional statements** run code only when a condition is true.
- Forms: `if`, `if-else`, `if-elif-else` ladder (Python) / `else if` (others), **nested if**, `switch` / `match`, and the **ternary** operator.
- Python uses indentation and a colon `:`; the others use `( )` around the condition and `{ }` braces.
- Only the **first** true branch runs.

code.sql:
SELECT name,
  CASE WHEN marks >= 90 THEN 'A'
       WHEN marks >= 60 THEN 'B'
       ELSE 'C' END AS grade
FROM students;

concepts.title: switch / match
concepts.text: `switch` picks a branch by comparing one value against many `case`s. **Remember `break`** in JS/Java/C++ — without it execution *falls through* into the next case. Python 3.10+ has `match`/`case`.

code.python:
day = 3
match day:
    case 1 | 7:
        print("Weekend")
    case 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6:
        print("Weekday")
    case _:
        print("Invalid")

concepts.title: Loops
concepts.text:
**Loops** repeat code.
- `for` — when you know how many times (or to walk over a collection).
- `while` — repeat while a condition is true (check first).
- `do-while` (JS/Java/C++) — runs the body **at least once**, checks after.
- **Nested loops** — a loop inside a loop; the inner loop finishes completely for every outer step (used in patterns and 2-D grids).
- `break` exits the loop; `continue` skips to the next iteration. Python also has `for…else` (the else runs if no `break` happened).
- Python `range(start, stop, step)` — `stop` is excluded.

code.python:
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i, end=" ")      # 1 2 3 4 5
print()
n = 5
while n > 0:
    n -= 2
print(n)                   # -1
for i in range(1, 4):      # nested: multiplication table
    for j in range(1, 4):
        print(i * j, end=" ")
    print()

concepts.title: break, continue and pass
concepts.text:
- `break` — leave the loop immediately.
- `continue` — skip the rest of this iteration and go to the next one.
- `pass` (Python only) — do nothing; a placeholder where a statement is required.

concepts.title: How to solve pattern problems
concepts.text:
**Recipe for any pattern:**
1. The **outer loop** controls the rows (`i` from 1 to n).
2. For each row, find **how many spaces and how many stars** in terms of `i` and `n` (make a small table for n = 4).
3. Inner loops (or string repetition) print spaces, then stars; then move to a new line.
4. Symmetric shapes (diamond, butterfly, hourglass, heart) = an upper half + a lower half.

Example row rules: pyramid → `n-i` spaces + `2i-1` stars; butterfly → `i` stars + `2(n-i)` spaces + `i` stars; rhombus → `n-i` spaces + `n` stars.

Ask me for a specific one, e.g. **"butterfly pattern in Java"**, **"heart pattern in C++"**, **"rhombus pattern in Python"**.

concepts.title: Functions
concepts.text:
A **function** (called a **method** in Java) is a named, reusable block of code. You **define** it once and **call** it many times.
- **Parameters** are the names in the definition; **arguments** are the values you pass.
- `return` sends a value back (a function without `return` gives `None` in Python / `undefined` in JS / `void` in Java & C++).
- Benefits: reuse, readability, easier testing.
- Ask me for **"types of functions"** to see every kind.

code.python:
def area(length, width=1):     # width has a default value
    return length * width

print(area(5, 3))   # 15
print(area(4))      # 4

concepts.title: Types of functions
concepts.text:
**By who wrote it**
- **Built-in** — provided by the language (`len`, `print`, `Math.max`, `strlen`).
- **User-defined** — written by you.

**By arguments & return value** (the classic 4 types)
1. No arguments, no return value
2. Arguments, no return value
3. No arguments, returns a value
4. Arguments **and** returns a value

**Special kinds**
- **Default / keyword arguments** (Python, JS, C++), **variable-length** arguments (`*args`, `**kwargs`, JS `...rest`, Java `int... nums`).
- **Anonymous / lambda / arrow** functions.
- **Recursive** functions — call themselves.
- **Higher-order** functions — take or return functions (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sorted(key=…)`).
- **Nested functions & closures**, **generators** (`yield`), **pure** functions (no side effects).
- Java/C++: **static vs instance** methods, **overloading** (same name, different parameters), **inline** & **pass by value / reference** (C++).

code.python:
def greet():                 # 1. no args, no return
    print("Hi")
def show(x):                 # 2. args, no return
    print(x)
def pi():                    # 3. no args, returns
    return 3.14
def add(a, b):               # 4. args + return
    return a + b
def total(*nums, **info):    # variable-length
    return sum(nums), info
square = lambda x: x * x     # anonymous
print(list(map(square, [1, 2, 3])))   # higher-order → [1, 4, 9]
print(total(1, 2, 3, city="Pune"))    # (6, {'city': 'Pune'})
code.javascript:
function greet() { console.log("Hi"); }
function add(a, b = 0) { return a + b; }        // default arg
const sum = (...nums) => nums.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0); // rest + arrow
const makeCounter = () => { let c = 0; return () => ++c; }; // closure
const next = makeCounter(); next(); console.log(next()); // 2
console.log([1, 2, 3].map((x) => x * x));              // higher-order
code.cpp:
void greet() { cout << "Hi"; }          // no args, no return
int add(int a, int b = 0) { return a + b; } // default argument
double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; } // overloading
void twice(int &x) { x *= 2; }          // pass by reference
inline int sq(int x) { return x * x; }  // inline
auto cube = [](int x) { return x * x * x; }; // lambda

concepts.title: Lambda, arrow & higher-order functions
concepts.text: A **lambda / arrow function** is a small unnamed function written inline. A **higher-order function** takes a function as an argument (or returns one) — `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sort` with a key. A function passed in is often called a **callback**.

code.python:
nums = [5, 2, 8, 1]
print(list(map(lambda x: x * 2, nums)))        # [10, 4, 16, 2]
print(list(filter(lambda x: x > 2, nums)))     # [5, 8]
from functools import reduce
print(reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, nums))        # 16
print(sorted(["pear", "fig", "apple"], key=len))  # ['fig', 'pear', 'apple']
code.javascript:
const nums = [5, 2, 8, 1];
console.log(nums.map((x) => x * 2));            // [10, 4, 16, 2]
console.log(nums.filter((x) => x > 2));         // [5, 8]
console.log(nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));   // 16
setTimeout(() => console.log("later"), 100);    // callback

concepts.title: Recursion
concepts.text:
**Recursion** = a function that calls itself on a smaller version of the problem.
Every recursive function needs:
1. A **base case** that stops the calls (otherwise: stack overflow / `RecursionError`).
2. A **recursive case** that moves toward the base case.

**Types of recursion**
- **Direct** — the function calls itself.
- **Indirect** — A calls B, B calls A.
- **Tail** — the recursive call is the *last* thing done (`return f(n-1, acc)`).
- **Head** — the recursive call happens *first*, work is done while returning.
- **Tree** — more than one call per step (Fibonacci `fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`).
- **Nested** — the argument itself is a recursive call (`f(f(n-1))`).

Classic problems: factorial, Fibonacci, sum of digits, power, reverse a string, palindrome check, GCD, binary search, Tower of Hanoi.

code.python:
def fact(n):                 # direct recursion
    if n <= 1:               # base case
        return 1
    return n * fact(n - 1)   # recursive case

def fib(n):                  # tree recursion
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

def fact_tail(n, acc=1):     # tail recursion
    return acc if n <= 1 else fact_tail(n - 1, acc * n)

print(fact(5), fib(7), fact_tail(5))   # 120 13 120
code.sql:
-- Recursive CTE: numbers 1..5
WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5
)
SELECT n FROM nums;

concepts.title: Classes & objects (OOP)
concepts.text:
**Object-oriented programming** groups data (attributes) and behaviour (methods) into **classes**. An **object** is one instance of a class.
- A **constructor** sets up a new object (`__init__` in Python, same-name method in Java/C++, `constructor` in JS).
- `self` (Python) / `this` (JS, Java, C++) refers to the current object.

**4 pillars:** Encapsulation (hide data, expose methods), Inheritance (a child class reuses a parent), Polymorphism (same method name, different behaviour), Abstraction (show only what is needed).

code.python:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, marks):   # constructor
        self.name = name
        self.marks = marks
    def grade(self):
        return "A" if self.marks >= 90 else "B"

s = Student("Asha", 93)
print(s.name, s.grade())   # Asha A

concepts.title: Inheritance & polymorphism
concepts.text:
- **Inheritance:** a child class gets the parent's attributes and methods (`class Dog(Animal)` / `extends` / `: public`).
- **Method overriding** (runtime polymorphism): the child redefines a parent method with the same signature.
- **Method overloading** (compile-time polymorphism, Java/C++): same name, different parameter lists.
- **Encapsulation:** keep fields private, access via methods (getters/setters).
- **Abstraction:** abstract classes / interfaces declare *what* to do, subclasses decide *how*.
- Types of inheritance: single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple (Python/C++; Java via interfaces), hybrid.

concepts.title: Exception handling
concepts.text:
An **exception** is an error that happens while the program runs. Handle it so the program does not crash:
- Python: `try / except / else / finally`, raise your own with `raise ValueError("…")`.
- JS / Java / C++: `try { } catch (e) { }`, Java & JS also have `finally`; throw with `throw`.
- `finally` always runs (cleanup: closing files, connections).

concepts.title: Pointers & references (C++)
concepts.text:
- A **pointer** stores a memory address: `int* p = &x;` — `&x` gives the address, `*p` reads/writes the value at it.
- A **reference** is another name for an existing variable: `int& r = x;` (cannot be null, cannot be re-seated).
- **Pass by value** copies the argument; **pass by reference** (`int& x`) lets the function change the caller's variable.
- Python, JS and Java pass *object references by value*: mutating a list/object inside a function is visible outside, but reassigning the parameter is not.

code.cpp:
int x = 10;
int* p = &x;      // p holds the address of x
*p = 20;          // changes x
int& r = x;       // r is another name for x
r++;
cout << x << endl; // 21

void byValue(int a) { a = 99; }   // caller unchanged
void byRef(int& a) { a = 99; }    // caller changed
code.python:
def change(lst):
    lst.append(4)     # visible outside
    lst = [0]         # rebinding: NOT visible outside
nums = [1, 2, 3]
change(nums)
print(nums)           # [1, 2, 3, 4]

concepts.title: var vs let vs const
concepts.text:
- `var` — function-scoped, hoisted (usable before its line as `undefined`), can be redeclared. Avoid in modern code.
- `let` — block-scoped, can be reassigned, not usable before declaration (temporal dead zone).
- `const` — block-scoped, **cannot be reassigned** (but a const object/array can still be mutated).
- **Hoisting:** declarations are moved to the top of their scope; function declarations are fully hoisted.

concepts.title: Promises and async/await
concepts.text:
JavaScript runs one thing at a time; slow work (timers, network) is **asynchronous**.
- A **Promise** represents a future value: pending → fulfilled / rejected. Use `.then()` / `.catch()`.
- `async` functions always return a Promise; `await` pauses inside them until the Promise settles.
- The **event loop** runs callbacks after the current code finishes — that is why `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs *after* synchronous logs.

concepts.title: Closures
concepts.text: A **closure** is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that outer function has returned. Used for counters, data privacy and function factories.

code.python:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return inc
c = make_counter(); c(); c()
print(c())   # 3

concepts.title: Java essentials
concepts.text:
- **JDK** (tools + compiler `javac`) ⊃ **JRE** (runtime) ⊃ **JVM** (runs bytecode). Java compiles to `.class` bytecode → "write once, run anywhere".
- `public static void main(String[] args)` is the entry point: `public` (callable by the JVM), `static` (no object needed), `void` (returns nothing).
- `static` members belong to the class, not to objects. `final` = cannot change (variable), cannot override (method), cannot extend (class).
- Access modifiers: `private` < default (package) < `protected` < `public`.
- **Wrapper classes** (`Integer`, `Double`, …) let primitives live in collections; conversion is automatic (autoboxing).

concepts.title: String vs StringBuilder (Java)
concepts.text: `String` is **immutable** — every `+` creates a new object, which is slow inside loops. `StringBuilder` is **mutable** and fast (`append`, `insert`, `reverse`, `deleteCharAt`). `StringBuffer` is the thread-safe (slower) version.

concepts.title: C++ essentials
concepts.text:
- `#include <iostream>` brings in `cin`/`cout`; `using namespace std;` lets you skip the `std::` prefix.
- Every program starts at `int main()`; `return 0;` means success.
- The **STL** gives ready containers (`vector`, `string`, `map`, `set`, `stack`, `queue`, `pair`), **algorithms** (`sort`, `reverse`, `find`, `count`, `max_element`, `binary_search`) and **iterators** (`v.begin()`, `v.end()`).
- `struct` members are public by default, `class` members are private by default.
- `auto` lets the compiler infer the type.

concepts.title: Python essentials
concepts.text:
- Python uses **indentation** (4 spaces) instead of braces — wrong indentation gives `IndentationError`.
- `None` means "no value" (like `null`).
- Handy built-ins: `len`, `range`, `enumerate` (index + value), `zip` (walk lists together), `sorted`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `abs`, `round`, `type`, `isinstance`.
- **f-strings** format text: `f"{name} scored {marks:.1f}"`.
- `import math` / `from random import randint` to use modules.

code.python:
names = ["asha", "ravi"]
marks = [91.5, 78]
for i, (n, m) in enumerate(zip(names, marks), start=1):
    print(f"{i}. {n.title()} scored {m:.1f}")
# 1. Asha scored 91.5
# 2. Ravi scored 78.0
import math
print(math.sqrt(16), round(3.14159, 2))  # 4.0 3.14

concepts.title: Generators & decorators
concepts.text:
- A **generator** function uses `yield` to produce values one at a time (lazy, memory-friendly).
- A **decorator** wraps a function to add behaviour: `@timer` above `def`.

concepts.title: File handling
concepts.text: Open a file, read or write, then close it. In Python use `with open(...)` so the file closes automatically. Modes: `"r"` read, `"w"` write (overwrites), `"a"` append.

code.python:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("line 1\nline 2\n")
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())
code.java:
Files.writeString(Path.of("notes.txt"), "line 1\n");
String text = Files.readString(Path.of("notes.txt"));

concepts.title: Time complexity (Big-O)
concepts.text:
**Big-O** describes how running time grows with input size *n*:
- `O(1)` constant — index into a list, dict lookup.
- `O(log n)` — binary search.
- `O(n)` — one loop over the data.
- `O(n log n)` — good sorting (merge sort, `sort()`).
- `O(n²)` — nested loops (bubble sort, most pattern programs).
- `O(2ⁿ)` — naive recursive Fibonacci.
Drop constants and keep the biggest term: `3n² + 5n` → `O(n²)`.

concepts.title: Linear vs binary search
concepts.text:
- **Linear search:** check each item one by one — `O(n)`, works on any list.
- **Binary search:** only on a **sorted** list; compare with the middle and discard half each step — `O(log n)`.

concepts.title: Sorting
concepts.text:
In real code use the built-in sort (`sorted()` / `list.sort()`, `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`, `Arrays.sort`, `std::sort`) — it is `O(n log n)`. For learning, **bubble sort** repeatedly swaps neighbours that are in the wrong order (`O(n²)`); **selection sort** picks the minimum each pass; **insertion sort** inserts each item into the sorted left part; **merge sort** and **quick sort** divide and conquer (`O(n log n)`).

JavaScript trap: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]` (it compares as strings) — always pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers.

concepts.title: Compiler vs interpreter
concepts.text:
- A **compiler** translates the whole program to machine code (or bytecode) before running — C++ (machine code), Java (bytecode for the JVM). Errors are reported before the program runs; execution is fast.
- An **interpreter** reads and runs the program line by line — Python, JavaScript (modern engines also use JIT compilation). Easier to experiment; errors appear when that line runs.

concepts.title: SQL sub-languages
concepts.text:
SQL commands are grouped into 5 sub-languages:
- **DDL** (Data Definition) — structure: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `RENAME`.
- **DML** (Data Manipulation) — rows: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` (`MERGE`).
- **DQL** (Data Query) — reading: `SELECT`.
- **DCL** (Data Control) — permissions: `GRANT`, `REVOKE`.
- **TCL** (Transaction Control) — `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`, (`BEGIN`/`START TRANSACTION`).
Tip: DDL commands auto-commit in MySQL/Oracle, so they usually cannot be rolled back.

concepts.title: DDL — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
concepts.text:
**DDL** defines or changes the *structure* of database objects.
- `CREATE TABLE` — make a table with columns, types and constraints.
- `ALTER TABLE` — add / drop / rename / modify columns.
- `DROP TABLE` — delete the table **and** its data completely.
- `TRUNCATE TABLE` — delete **all rows** quickly but keep the structure.

concepts.title: Constraints & keys
concepts.text:
**Constraints** are rules that keep data valid:
- `PRIMARY KEY` — uniquely identifies each row (unique + not null, one per table, may be composite).
- `FOREIGN KEY` — a column that must match a primary key in another table (referential integrity). `ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes child rows automatically.
- `UNIQUE` — no duplicates (NULLs allowed). `NOT NULL` — value required. `CHECK` — condition must be true. `DEFAULT` — value used when none is given.

concepts.title: DML — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
concepts.text:
**DML** changes the *rows* inside tables.
- `INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (...)` — add rows (many rows in one statement is allowed).
- `UPDATE t SET col = value WHERE ...` — change rows. **Forgetting `WHERE` updates every row!**
- `DELETE FROM t WHERE ...` — remove rows (without `WHERE` it removes all rows, but can be rolled back inside a transaction, unlike `TRUNCATE`).

concepts.title: DQL — SELECT and filtering
concepts.text:
`SELECT` reads data. Clause order: **SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT**.
- `WHERE` filters rows: `=`, `<>`, `>`, `BETWEEN a AND b` (inclusive), `IN (...)`, `LIKE 'A%'` (`%` any chars, `_` one char), `IS NULL` (never `= NULL`).
- `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows. `AS` gives an alias. `ORDER BY col DESC` sorts. `LIMIT n OFFSET k` pages results.

code.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students;
SELECT name, age AS years
FROM students
WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 25
  AND name LIKE 'A%'
  AND email IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age DESC, name
LIMIT 5;

concepts.title: Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
concepts.text:
**Aggregate functions** summarise many rows into one value: `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(col)` (ignores NULL), `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`.
- `GROUP BY col` makes one result row per group.
- `HAVING` filters **groups** (after aggregation); `WHERE` filters **rows** (before). You cannot use aggregates in `WHERE`.
- Every selected column must be either grouped or aggregated.

code.sql:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS staff, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 20000        -- rows first
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3        -- then groups
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;

concepts.title: JOINs
concepts.text:
A **JOIN** combines rows from two tables using a related column.
- `INNER JOIN` — only rows that match in **both** tables.
- `LEFT JOIN` — **all** rows from the left table + matches from the right (NULL where no match).
- `RIGHT JOIN` — all rows from the right table + matches from the left.
- `FULL OUTER JOIN` — all rows from both sides.
- `CROSS JOIN` — every combination (m × n rows).
- **Self join** — a table joined with itself (e.g. employee → manager).

code.sql:
-- employees with their department name (only matching rows)
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id;

-- every department, even ones with no employees
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS staff
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.name;

-- self join: employee and manager
SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;

concepts.title: Subqueries & set operations
concepts.text:
- A **subquery** is a SELECT inside another query (in `WHERE`, `FROM` or `SELECT`). A **correlated** subquery refers to the outer row and runs once per row.
- `EXISTS (subquery)` is true if the subquery returns any row.
- **Set operations** combine results of queries with the same number of columns: `UNION` (removes duplicates), `UNION ALL` (keeps them), `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` / `MINUS`.
- A **CTE** (`WITH name AS (...)`) names a subquery to make long queries readable.

concepts.title: SQL built-in functions
concepts.text:
- **String:** `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `LENGTH`, `SUBSTR(s, start, len)`, `TRIM`, `REPLACE`, `CONCAT` / `||`, `INSTR`.
- **Numeric:** `ROUND(x, d)`, `ABS`, `CEIL`, `FLOOR`, `MOD`.
- **Date:** `CURRENT_DATE`, `NOW()`, `DATE()`, `strftime` (SQLite), `YEAR()` (MySQL).
- **NULL handling:** `COALESCE(a, b, …)` returns the first non-NULL; `IFNULL` / `NVL`.

code.sql:
SELECT UPPER(name), LENGTH(name), SUBSTR(name, 1, 3),
       ROUND(salary / 12, 2) AS monthly,
       COALESCE(phone, 'not given') AS phone
FROM employees;

concepts.title: TCL — transactions
concepts.text:
A **transaction** is a group of statements that succeed or fail **together**.
- `BEGIN` / `START TRANSACTION` — start.
- `COMMIT` — make all changes permanent.
- `ROLLBACK` — undo everything since the start (or since a savepoint: `ROLLBACK TO sp`).
- `SAVEPOINT sp` — a checkpoint inside a transaction.

**ACID:** Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules always hold), Isolation (transactions do not disturb each other), Durability (committed data survives crashes).

concepts.title: DCL — GRANT and REVOKE
concepts.text:
**DCL** controls who may do what.
- `GRANT privilege ON object TO user` — give permission (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `ALL PRIVILEGES`…).
- `REVOKE privilege ON object FROM user` — take it back.
- `WITH GRANT OPTION` lets that user grant the privilege to others.
- Roles group privileges: `CREATE ROLE analyst; GRANT SELECT ON sales TO analyst; GRANT analyst TO ravi;`
(SQLite has no users, so in the games DCL questions are concept-based; the syntax below is MySQL/PostgreSQL.)

concepts.title: Views, indexes & window functions
concepts.text:
- A **view** is a saved SELECT that behaves like a virtual table (`CREATE VIEW … AS SELECT …`).
- An **index** speeds up searches on a column (like a book index) but slows down inserts/updates slightly.
- **Window functions** compute over a set of rows *without* collapsing them: `ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()` (gaps after ties), `DENSE_RANK()` (no gaps), `SUM() OVER (...)`, `LAG`, `LEAD`. `PARTITION BY` restarts the calculation for each group.

concepts.title: Normalization
concepts.text:
**Normalization** organises tables to remove duplicate data and update anomalies.
- **1NF:** each cell holds one atomic value; no repeating groups.
- **2NF:** 1NF + every non-key column depends on the **whole** primary key (no partial dependency).
- **3NF:** 2NF + no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency).
- **BCNF:** every determinant is a candidate key.

concepts.title: NULL / None / undefined
concepts.text:
- **SQL `NULL`** means "unknown". Any comparison with NULL is unknown, so use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`; aggregates like `AVG` skip NULLs.
- **Python** uses `None`; test with `x is None`.
- **JavaScript** has `undefined` (declared but no value) and `null` (intentionally empty); `null == undefined` is true, `null === undefined` is false. `NaN` ("not a number") is not equal even to itself — use `Number.isNaN`.
- **Java** `null` for references → `NullPointerException` if you call a method on it. **C++** uses `nullptr` for pointers.

comparisons.title: List vs tuple
comparisons.text:
| | List | Tuple |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `[1, 2]` | `(1, 2)` |
| Mutable? | Yes | **No** |
| Methods | many (`append`, `sort`…) | only `count`, `index` |
| Speed / memory | slower, more memory | faster, less memory |
| Dict key? | No | Yes (if items are immutable) |
Use a **tuple** for fixed data (coordinates, days of week) and a **list** when items change.

comparisons.title: List vs set
comparisons.text:
- **List:** ordered, allows duplicates, indexable (`lst[0]`).
- **Set:** unordered, **unique** items only, no indexing, very fast `in` checks, supports union/intersection.
`list(set(lst))` removes duplicates (order not guaranteed; use `list(dict.fromkeys(lst))` to keep order).

comparisons.title: List vs dictionary
comparisons.text:
- **List:** values accessed by numeric position `lst[2]`.
- **Dictionary:** values accessed by a **key** `d["name"]`; keys are unique; lookup is O(1) on average.
Use a dict when each value has a meaningful label.

comparisons.title: Tuple vs set
comparisons.text:
- **Tuple:** ordered, immutable, duplicates allowed, indexable.
- **Set:** unordered, mutable (you can add/remove), **unique** items, not indexable.

comparisons.title: append() vs extend()
comparisons.text:
- `append(x)` adds **one** item (even if it is a list → nested): `[1, 2].append([3, 4])` → `[1, 2, [3, 4]]`.
- `extend(iterable)` adds **each** item: `[1, 2].extend([3, 4])` → `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

comparisons.title: remove() vs pop() vs del
comparisons.text:
- `remove(x)` deletes the first item **equal to x** (ValueError if missing), returns None.
- `pop(i)` deletes by **index** (default last) and **returns** the item.
- `del lst[i]` / `del lst[a:b]` deletes by index or slice, returns nothing.

comparisons.title: sort() vs sorted()
comparisons.text:
- `lst.sort()` sorts the list **in place** and returns `None`.
- `sorted(iterable)` returns a **new** sorted list and works on any iterable (strings, tuples, dicts).
Both accept `key=` and `reverse=True`.

comparisons.title: == vs is (Python)
comparisons.text:
- `==` compares **values** (are they equal?).
- `is` compares **identity** (are they the same object in memory?).
`[1] == [1]` → True but `[1] is [1]` → False. Use `is` only for `None`: `if x is None`.

comparisons.title: == vs === (JavaScript)
comparisons.text:
- `==` (loose) converts types before comparing: `5 == "5"` → true, `0 == false` → true.
- `===` (strict) needs the same type **and** value: `5 === "5"` → false.
Always prefer `===`.

comparisons.title: var vs let vs const
comparisons.text:
| | var | let | const |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | function | block | block |
| Reassign | yes | yes | **no** |
| Redeclare | yes | no | no |
| Hoisted usable before line | yes (`undefined`) | no (TDZ) | no (TDZ) |

comparisons.title: null vs undefined
comparisons.text:
- `undefined`: a variable exists but has no value yet (also missing properties, functions with no return).
- `null`: a value you set on purpose to mean "empty".
`typeof undefined` → "undefined", `typeof null` → "object" (a historic bug). `null == undefined` true, `===` false.

comparisons.title: for vs while loop
comparisons.text:
- Use **for** when the number of iterations is known or you walk over a collection.
- Use **while** when you repeat until a condition changes (unknown count), e.g. reading input until "quit".
Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop.

comparisons.title: while vs do-while
comparisons.text:
- `while` checks the condition **first** — the body may run 0 times.
- `do { } while (cond);` checks **after** — the body always runs **at least once**. (Python has no do-while.)

comparisons.title: break vs continue
comparisons.text:
- `break` **exits** the whole loop.
- `continue` **skips** only the current iteration and continues with the next one.

comparisons.title: Recursion vs iteration
comparisons.text:
- **Recursion:** a function calls itself; elegant for trees, divide & conquer, backtracking; uses the call stack (risk of stack overflow), usually slower.
- **Iteration:** loops; uses constant extra memory and is usually faster.
Every recursive solution can be written iteratively (sometimes with an explicit stack).

comparisons.title: Parameter vs argument
comparisons.text:
- **Parameter:** the variable name in the function **definition** — `def add(a, b)`.
- **Argument:** the actual value passed in the **call** — `add(2, 3)`.

comparisons.title: Call by value vs call by reference
comparisons.text:
- **By value:** the function gets a **copy**; changes do not affect the caller (`void f(int x)` in C++, all primitives in Java).
- **By reference:** the function works on the **original** (`void f(int& x)` in C++).
Java/Python/JS pass object references by value: you can mutate the object, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

comparisons.title: Method overloading vs overriding
comparisons.text:
| | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| Where | same class | parent → child class |
| Signature | **different** parameters | **same** signature |
| Polymorphism | compile-time | runtime |
| Example | `add(int,int)` & `add(double,double)` | `Dog.speak()` replaces `Animal.speak()` |

comparisons.title: Class vs object
comparisons.text:
- A **class** is the blueprint (e.g. `Car` with fields `color`, `speed` and method `drive()`).
- An **object** is a real instance built from it (`myCar = Car("red")`). One class → many objects.

comparisons.title: Abstract class vs interface (Java)
comparisons.text:
- **Abstract class:** can have fields, constructors, and both abstract and concrete methods; a class can extend only **one**.
- **Interface:** a contract of methods (plus default/static methods); a class can implement **many**.
Use an interface for "can do" (Comparable, Runnable), an abstract class for a shared base with common code.

comparisons.title: Array vs ArrayList (Java)
comparisons.text:
- **Array:** fixed size, can hold primitives (`int[]`), `a.length`, fast.
- **ArrayList:** grows automatically, holds objects only (`ArrayList<Integer>`), `list.size()`, methods `add/get/set/remove/contains`.

comparisons.title: Array vs vector (C++)
comparisons.text:
- **Array** `int a[5]`: fixed size known at compile time, no size() method.
- **vector** `vector<int> v`: dynamic size (`push_back`, `pop_back`), knows its `size()`, works with STL algorithms. Prefer `vector`.

comparisons.title: String vs StringBuilder (Java)
comparisons.text:
- `String` is **immutable** — each change makes a new object (slow in loops).
- `StringBuilder` is **mutable** — `append`, `insert`, `reverse` modify it in place (fast). `StringBuffer` is the synchronized version.

comparisons.title: map vs unordered_map (C++)
comparisons.text:
- `map`: keys kept **sorted** (red-black tree), operations O(log n).
- `unordered_map`: no order (hash table), average O(1), worst O(n).

comparisons.title: Pointer vs reference (C++)
comparisons.text:
- **Pointer** `int* p`: holds an address, can be null, can be re-pointed, needs `*` to access, supports arithmetic.
- **Reference** `int& r`: an alias, must be initialised, cannot be null or re-bound, used like the variable itself.

comparisons.title: struct vs class (C++)
comparisons.text: They are almost identical in C++; the only difference is the default access: `struct` members are **public** by default, `class` members are **private** by default. By convention, use `struct` for plain data and `class` for objects with behaviour.

comparisons.title: Compiler vs interpreter
comparisons.text:
- **Compiler:** translates the whole program before running (C++, Java→bytecode); errors listed up front; fast execution.
- **Interpreter:** translates and runs line by line (Python, JavaScript); stops at the first runtime error; quicker to try things.

comparisons.title: Python vs Java
comparisons.text:
- **Python:** dynamically typed, indentation-based, very short code, interpreted; great for beginners, data science, automation.
- **Java:** statically typed, braces + semicolons, compiled to JVM bytecode, verbose but fast and strict; used for Android, enterprise back-ends.

comparisons.title: Java vs JavaScript
comparisons.text:
Despite the name they are unrelated languages.
- **Java:** statically typed, compiled to bytecode, class-based, runs on the JVM.
- **JavaScript:** dynamically typed, interpreted/JIT, runs in browsers and Node.js, prototype-based objects, first-class functions.

comparisons.title: C vs C++
comparisons.text:
- **C:** procedural, no classes, `printf/scanf`, manual memory with `malloc/free`.
- **C++:** C plus OOP (classes, inheritance), templates, the STL, references, `cin/cout`, `new/delete`, exceptions.

comparisons.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
comparisons.text:
| | DELETE | TRUNCATE | DROP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type | DML | DDL | DDL |
| Removes | chosen rows (`WHERE`) | **all** rows | whole table (structure + data) |
| WHERE allowed | yes | no | no |
| Rollback | yes (in a transaction) | usually no | usually no |
| Speed | slower (row by row) | fast | fast |

comparisons.title: WHERE vs HAVING
comparisons.text:
- `WHERE` filters **rows before** grouping; cannot use aggregate functions.
- `HAVING` filters **groups after** `GROUP BY`; can use aggregates (`HAVING COUNT(*) > 2`).
A query can use both: `WHERE salary > 0 GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000`.

comparisons.title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN
comparisons.text:
- `INNER JOIN` returns only rows with a match in **both** tables.
- `LEFT JOIN` returns **every** row of the left table; columns from the right are NULL when there is no match. Use it to find "customers with no orders" (`WHERE o.id IS NULL`).

comparisons.title: Primary key vs foreign key
comparisons.text:
- **Primary key:** uniquely identifies each row of *its own* table; unique + NOT NULL; one per table.
- **Foreign key:** a column that points to the primary key of *another* table; can repeat and can be NULL; enforces referential integrity.

comparisons.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE
comparisons.text:
- **PRIMARY KEY:** only one per table, never NULL.
- **UNIQUE:** many per table allowed, NULL values allowed (in most databases).

comparisons.title: CHAR vs VARCHAR
comparisons.text:
- `CHAR(n)`: fixed length — always uses n characters (padded with spaces). Good for fixed codes like `CHAR(2)` state codes.
- `VARCHAR(n)`: variable length up to n — stores only what you type. Good for names, emails.

comparisons.title: UNION vs UNION ALL
comparisons.text:
- `UNION` combines results and **removes duplicates** (slower, extra sort).
- `UNION ALL` keeps **all** rows including duplicates (faster).

comparisons.title: COMMIT vs ROLLBACK
comparisons.text:
- `COMMIT` saves all changes of the current transaction permanently.
- `ROLLBACK` cancels all changes since the transaction began (or since a SAVEPOINT).

comparisons.title: GRANT vs REVOKE
comparisons.text:
- `GRANT` gives a privilege to a user/role: `GRANT SELECT ON emp TO ravi;`
- `REVOKE` takes it away: `REVOKE SELECT ON emp FROM ravi;`
Both are DCL commands.

comparisons.title: DDL vs DML
comparisons.text:
- **DDL** changes the **structure** (tables, columns): `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`; auto-committed in most databases.
- **DML** changes the **data** (rows): `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; can be rolled back inside a transaction.

comparisons.title: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
comparisons.text:
For scores 90, 90, 80:
- `ROW_NUMBER()` → 1, 2, 3 (always unique)
- `RANK()` → 1, 1, **3** (gap after a tie)
- `DENSE_RANK()` → 1, 1, **2** (no gap)

comparisons.title: Stack vs queue
comparisons.text:
- **Stack:** LIFO — the last item pushed is the first popped (undo button, function call stack).
- **Queue:** FIFO — the first item added is the first removed (print jobs, BFS).

comparisons.title: Linear vs binary search
comparisons.text:
- **Linear:** checks every element, works on unsorted data, O(n).
- **Binary:** needs **sorted** data, halves the range each step, O(log n).

comparisons.title: Mutable vs immutable
comparisons.text:
- **Mutable** objects can change after creation: Python `list`, `dict`, `set`; JS arrays/objects; Java `StringBuilder`, `ArrayList`.
- **Immutable** objects cannot: Python `int`, `float`, `str`, `tuple`, `frozenset`; Java `String`; JS primitives.
"Changing" an immutable value actually creates a new object.

comparisons.title: Local vs global variables
comparisons.text:
- **Local:** created inside a function, only visible there, destroyed when it returns.
- **Global:** created outside functions, visible everywhere in the file. In Python you need `global name` to *reassign* it inside a function.

comparisons.title: print vs return
comparisons.text:
- `print` only **shows** a value on the screen.
- `return` **sends** a value back to the caller so it can be stored or used (`total = add(2, 3)`). A function that only prints returns `None`.

errors.pattern: indentationerror|unexpected indent|expected an indented block|unindent does not match
errors.title: IndentationError
errors.text:
Python uses indentation to know which lines belong to a block.
- After every line ending in `:` (`if`, `for`, `while`, `def`, `class`) the next line must be indented (4 spaces).
- Lines in the same block must line up exactly — don't mix tabs and spaces.

errors.title: SyntaxError
errors.text:
The code breaks Python's grammar. Most common causes:
- Missing colon `:` after `if/for/while/def/else`.
- Using `=` instead of `==` inside a condition.
- Unclosed brackets or quotes (the error often points at the *next* line).
- Writing `else if` instead of `elif`.

errors.title: NameError / "is not defined"
errors.text:
You used a name Python/JavaScript doesn't know:
- A typo in the variable/function name (names are case-sensitive: `Total` ≠ `total`).
- Using a variable before assigning it, or outside its scope.
- Forgetting quotes around text: `print(hello)` instead of `print("hello")`.
- Forgetting an import (`math.sqrt` without `import math`).

errors.pattern: typeerror.*(concatenate|can only concatenate|unsupported operand|must be str)
errors.title: TypeError: can only concatenate str
errors.text:
You tried to combine a `str` with a number: `"Age: " + 21`.
Fix: convert first — `"Age: " + str(21)` — or use an f-string: `f"Age: {21}"`.

errors.title: TypeError: object is not subscriptable
errors.text: You used `[ ]` on something that isn't a sequence/mapping — often an `int` or `None`. Check what the variable really contains with `print(type(x))`. A common cause: `x = lst.sort()` (sort returns None).

errors.title: TypeError / AttributeError with 'NoneType'
errors.text: A variable is `None` where you expected a value. Usually a function has no `return`, or you stored the result of an in-place method (`lst = lst.sort()`, `lst = lst.append(x)` — both return None).

errors.pattern: typeerror.*(missing \d+ required positional argument|takes \d+ positional argument)
errors.title: TypeError: wrong number of arguments
errors.text: The call passes a different number of arguments than the function defines. Compare `def f(a, b)` with the call `f(1)`. Inside a class, remember the first parameter `self`.

errors.pattern: indexerror|index out of range|arrayindexoutofboundsexception|out_of_range|index \d+ out of bounds
errors.title: Index out of range
errors.text:
You accessed a position that doesn't exist. Valid indexes are `0` to `len - 1`.
- Loop with `range(len(lst))`, not `range(len(lst) + 1)`; in Java/C++ use `i < n`, not `i <= n`.
- An empty list has no `lst[0]`.

errors.title: KeyError
errors.text: The dictionary has no such key. Use `d.get(key, default)` or check with `if key in d:` first. Remember keys are case-sensitive.

errors.title: ValueError: invalid literal for int()
errors.text: `int()` got text that isn't a whole number (e.g. `"12.5"`, `"abc"`, `""`). Use `float()` for decimals, strip spaces, or wrap in `try/except ValueError`.

errors.title: Division by zero
errors.text: You divided by 0. Check the divisor first: `if b != 0:`. (JavaScript returns `Infinity` instead of throwing; C++ integer division by zero crashes.)

errors.title: AttributeError
errors.text: The object has no such method/attribute — e.g. `"abc".push()` (strings have no push), `lst.length` (use `len(lst)`), or a typo like `.apend`. Use `dir(obj)` to list what exists.

errors.title: ModuleNotFoundError
errors.text: The module isn't installed or the name is misspelled. Install it with `pip install name` and check the spelling. Don't name your own file the same as a module (e.g. `random.py`).

errors.title: Stack overflow (too deep recursion)
errors.text:
A recursive function keeps calling itself without stopping. Check that:
1. There is a **base case**.
2. Every call moves **toward** it (e.g. `n - 1`, not `n`).
3. The input can actually reach it (negative numbers?).

errors.title: ReferenceError
errors.text: JavaScript can't find that variable — a typo, it is out of scope, or you used a `let`/`const` before its declaration line (temporal dead zone).

errors.title: TypeError: x is not a function
errors.text: You called something that isn't a function — a typo (`arr.lenght()`), calling a property (`arr.length()` — length is not a function), or using an array method on a non-array (e.g. `.map` on an object or a string).

errors.title: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
errors.text: You accessed `.something` on a value that is `undefined`/`null` — maybe an array index past the end, a missing object key, or data that hasn't loaded yet. Use optional chaining `obj?.prop` or check first.

errors.title: NullPointerException
errors.text: You called a method or accessed a field on a reference that is `null` — an object that was never created with `new`, an uninitialised array element, or a map `get()` that returned null. Initialise objects and check `if (x != null)`.

errors.title: error: cannot find symbol
errors.text: The compiler doesn't know a name: a typo (Java is case-sensitive: `string` vs `String`, `system` vs `System`), a variable used outside its block, or a missing `import` (e.g. `import java.util.*;` for `ArrayList`, `Scanner`).

errors.title: NumberFormatException
errors.text: `Integer.parseInt()` got text that isn't a valid integer (spaces, decimals, letters, empty string). Trim it and validate, or catch the exception.

errors.title: ClassCastException
errors.text: You cast an object to a type it isn't (e.g. `(String) someInteger`). Check with `instanceof` before casting, and use generics (`ArrayList<String>`) to avoid raw types.

errors.title: missing return statement
errors.text: A non-void method has a path that ends without `return`. Make sure every `if/else` branch returns, or add a final `return` after the if-block.

errors.title: incompatible types / lossy conversion
errors.text: You assigned a value of a wider type into a narrower one (`int x = 3.5;`, `int y = someLong;`). Cast explicitly `(int) 3.5` if that's what you want, or change the variable's type.

errors.title: Missing semicolon
errors.text: Java, C++ and (optionally) JavaScript end statements with `;`. The error usually points to the line **after** the missing semicolon — check the end of the previous line.

errors.title: Segmentation fault
errors.text:
The program touched memory it shouldn't:
- Array/vector index out of range (`v[n]` when size is n).
- Dereferencing a null or uninitialised pointer.
- Infinite recursion (stack overflow).
- Using memory after `delete`.
Tip: use `v.at(i)` instead of `v[i]` to get a clear exception.

errors.pattern: was not declared in this scope|not declared
errors.title: 'x' was not declared in this scope
errors.text: The compiler can't see that name: a typo, a missing `#include` (e.g. `<vector>`, `<algorithm>`, `<string>`), forgetting `std::` / `using namespace std;`, or using a variable outside the `{ }` where it was declared.

errors.title: undefined reference (linker error)
errors.text: A function was declared but never defined (or the file defining it wasn't compiled/linked). Check the spelling and signature match exactly, and that `main` exists.

errors.title: no such table
errors.text: The table doesn't exist (yet): check the spelling, the database you are connected to, and that `CREATE TABLE` ran first.

errors.pattern: no such column|unknown column|invalid column name
errors.title: no such column
errors.text: Check the column spelling and table alias. Text values need single quotes: `WHERE name = 'Asha'` — without quotes SQL thinks `Asha` is a column. Also, column aliases from SELECT can't be used in WHERE.

errors.title: UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY violation
errors.text: You inserted a value that already exists in a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE column. Use a different value, `UPDATE` the existing row, or `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` / `INSERT IGNORE`.

errors.pattern: not null constraint failed|cannot be null
errors.title: NOT NULL constraint failed
errors.text: A NOT NULL column didn't get a value. Include that column in your INSERT or give it a DEFAULT.

errors.pattern: foreign key constraint failed|foreign key constraint fails
errors.title: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
errors.text: The value doesn't exist in the parent table (or you deleted a parent that still has children). Insert the parent row first, or use `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

errors.title: ambiguous column name
errors.text: Both joined tables have that column. Prefix it with the table or alias: `e.dept_id` instead of `dept_id`.

errors.pattern: must appear in the group by|not a group by expression|misuse of aggregate
errors.title: GROUP BY / aggregate error
errors.text: Every column in SELECT must be inside an aggregate or listed in GROUP BY. And aggregates can't go in WHERE — use HAVING instead.

errors.pattern: near ".*": syntax error|syntax error at or near|you have an error in your sql syntax
errors.title: SQL syntax error
errors.text: Look just before the word mentioned in the error. Common causes: missing comma between columns, a trailing comma before `FROM`, wrong clause order (WHERE must come before GROUP BY/ORDER BY), double quotes instead of single quotes for text, or a reserved word used as a name.
